newsitem.title: USA: "Shine" pianist makes New York debut.
newsitem.headline: "Shine" pianist makes New York debut.

text.p: Australian pianist David Helfgott played Beethoven at his long-awaited New York debut Tuesday night and the critics were unanimous -- Beethoven and music lost.

But a sell-out crowd of more than 2,000 people at Avery Fischer Hall gave the pianist, whose comeback from mental breakdown inspired the hit film "Shine," five standing ovations, several sustained bursts of applause and more than a scattering of cheers in what was clearly a "feel-good" evening for them.

New York, the sixth stop of Helfgott's 19-concert first-ever North American tour, followed a pattern that started with his first concert in Boston in early March. The critics were hostile and the audience enraptured, talking among themselves at intermission about how many times they have seen the film and some even boasting that they were taking part in history.

The star ran on and off stage in a flowing white blouse with frilly cuffs following signals from off-stage. He raced through his performance, groaning, singing and talking to himself and sometimes to the piano keys, just as he does in Scott Hicks' film, which has been nominated for seven Oscars.
The film and Helfgott have become so popular the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has been busy denying that the pianist will make a suprise appearance at Monday's Oscar awards ceremony.
When his New York performance was over, Helfgott literally jumped for joy on the stage of Avery Fisher Hall, muttering to himself, "Take a bow, take a bow."

But critics, in review after review on Wednesday, said he should take a hike. They blasted his playing and wondered if the tour was really just a vehicle to exploit a mentally ill man and boost a film as Academy Awards voters make up their minds.

Concert-goers said in interviews after Tuesday's performance that it did not matter to them that his interpretation of Beethoven's "Appassionata" sonata was to pound the keyboards and groan. They were coming to see a triumph of the human spirit.
As lawyer Sidney Bernstein said, "The audience is cheering for this man and for the human spirit. We know what he overcame and it was a wonderful experience just to hear him."
The critics are just being too hard, he added.

But New York Daily News critic Terry Teachout said the harsh reviews have a point -- to bring audiences to their senses. In New York, as in earlier stops, Helfgott's show sold out to thousands of people paying up to $50 per ticket.

"What I am saying ... is that he can play this music in the limited sense that he can push down the keys in the right order but it is totally disconnected from any sense of musicality. His hands remember how to play the notes but his phrasing is bizarre. He sounded and looked like a gifted but uninhibited child," Teachout said.
Many professional musicians at the concert were angry at the performance and violinist Isaac Stern departed at intermission, declining a New York Times reporter's request for comment.
In the film, Stern is shown inviting a then 14-year-old Helfgott to the United States as a prodigy, but the violinist said he did not remember such an incident.

Pianist Carol Aicher said, "His playing was very amateurish. There are conservatory students who can't get a chance to play in concert halls and yet he is here. This is all about money and marketing."

Another musican wondered if the audience would play $50 a ticket to see the "Wheelchair Olympics, which is also a triumph of the human spirit. His problem is that he keeps his foot on the piano's footpedal and it's full-speed ahead. I can hear his mother shouting, 'Stop that banging.'"
